---
title: "Grad speech"
format: pdf
---

Good afternoon, graduates, families, faculty, and friends. Welcome is one of the finest moments in the life of our department — the moment we send you out into the world.


When you arrived at Duke, you came with priors. Some of you believed statistics was mostly about means and standard deviations. Some of you believed you'd never survive a measure theory course. Some of you — I suspect — believed your instructors or advisors were unreasonably demanding. Those priors have all been updated.


That, in essence, occasionally exhilarating process of Bayesian updating. You walk in with a prior. The data — the coursework, the 2 a.m. debugging sessions, qualifying exams the small triumphs — all of it is likelihood. And you walk out today as the posterior. Wiser. More calibrated. With appropriately wider uncertainty intervals in some places, and beautifully tighter ones in others.

You don't need certainty to do great work. You need honesty about your uncertainty, and the courage to put your model forward anyway.

The world you are entering desperately needs people who can do exactly that. We live in an era drowning in data and starving for wisdom. There are claims made every day with false precision — point estimates dressed up as truth, confidence confused with calibration. You have been trained to do something different. You have been trained to say: here is what I know, here is what I don't know, here is my best inference, and here is how I would change my mind. That is not weakness. That is the most rigorous form of intellectual honesty there is.

Some of you are heading to academia, where you will build the next generation of  theory and methods — tools we cannot yet imagine, solving problems we haven't yet named. Some of you are heading to industry, to government, to medicine, to policy — places where a well-reasoned posterior can change a decision, a drug, a life. 

Wherever you go, remember: you are not just statisticians and data scientists. You are translators between uncertainty and action. That is a rare and valuable thing.


To the families in the room — thank you. You have supported these students through the long nights of qualifying exams, through the semesters where the only update their prior received was this is harder than I thought. Your belief in them, even when theirs wavered, was its own kind of prior — strong, informative, and well-placed.

And to our graduates: you leave here with something no dataset can fully capture — a way of thinking. A discipline of mind. The ability to hold uncertainty and rigor in the same hand.
Go forth. Collect data. Update your beliefs. Be wrong sometimes, gracefully. Be right when it matters. And remember that the best models are not the ones that are always certain — they are the ones that are honestly uncertain, and useful anyway.

Congratulations, Class of 2025. The posterior looks excellent.
